explanation: Fred Lorz climbed into a car when cramp struck, rode a long stretch, then ran back into the stadium. He was found out and disqualified, and the gold went to Thomas Hicks.
learnMore: Athletics at the 1904 Summer Olympics - Men's marathon

claims.text: At the 1904 Olympic marathon in St. Louis, Fred Lorz, the first runner to reach the finish, had travelled part of the course in a car.
Lorz stopped running because of cramp and accepted a ride in a car before rejoining the race on foot.
Lorz was disqualified once officials learned of the car ride.
Thomas Hicks of the United States was awarded the gold medal in the 1904 Olympic marathon.

evidence.restatement: Fred Lorz was first into the stadium in the St Louis 1904 marathon, but he had been driven for a large chunk of the route (about 11 miles) in his manager's car.

claimResults.note: Answered True cold. One of the best-documented episodes in early Olympic history. Counterintuitive key carried under memo 18 by direct certain confirmation.

evidence.restatement: Suffering cramps around nine miles in, Lorz got into a car, rode for miles, and resumed running after the car broke down.

claimResults.note: Standard account (cramps/exhaustion, car ride, resumed on foot).

evidence.restatement: When officials discovered the ride, Lorz lost the win and was banned by the AAU (the ban was later lifted).
The 1904 marathon title went to Thomas Hicks, running for the USA.

claimResults.note: Hicks (English-born, competing for the United States) is the recorded champion. Certain.

evidence.restatement: Fred Lorz of the USA was first into the St. Louis stadium in 1904 after riding in a car for roughly eleven miles of the course.

claimResults.note: Rival test: 'the man who crossed the line in front' is Lorz (not Hicks, who was the first legitimate finisher). Hicks was never given a ride, only stimulants, so no second reading makes the statement false. Lorz called it a joke.

evidence.restatement: Lorz seized up with cramps about nine miles in, took a lift, and then jogged on when the car broke down.

claimResults.note: The car broke down near the end of his ride and he resumed on foot. Claim is consistent with that.

evidence.restatement: Officials removed Lorz from the results once his ride came out, and he was initially banned, later forgiven.

claimResults.note: The ban was lifted and he won the 1905 Boston Marathon; not needed for the claim.

evidence.restatement: After Lorz was thrown out, Thomas Hicks of the United States was declared the 1904 marathon champion.

claimResults.note: Flagged high only as a 'number' reason; it is a medal-winner fact. Hicks was born in England but represented the USA, so 'of the United States' is right.

stem: The man who crossed the line in front at the 1904 Olympic marathon had ridden part of the course in a car.
